events.text: A court painter from the Office of Painting comes up the valley with a servant, a folding stool and a box of brushes. The heir is to be invested in the spring, and the old qilin banner is so eaten by moths that the beast on it has three legs. Nobody alive has seen a qilin, so the painter has come to the cave where the old books say one was born, to sit by the rapids and hope.

choices.text: Come to the water at dawn and drink, and let the painter look

effects.log: The painter drops the brush in the rapids and does not go after it. You drink slowly. When you lift your head the painter is drawing with a finger in the wet sand, fast, before it can go.

choices.text: Stay hidden, but leave a shed scale and a line of hoofprints on the bank

effects.log: In the morning the painter finds one scale, blue at the root and yellow at the edge, and hoofprints in the mud that end at the water and do not come out again. The painter sits with them all day and draws nothing, and is happy.

choices.text: Let the painter go home with nothing. A banner is a thing kings carry

effects.log: The painter waits ten days and goes home and copies the moth-eaten banner, with four legs. The heir is invested under a beast that looks like a worried dog. Nobody at court notices but the painter.

choices.text: It is a hard age. Show yourself only for the space of a breath, on the far bank

effects.log: One breath, on the far bank, in the mist. It is enough for the painter and too much for the age: the servant talks in the inn on the way home, and by the new moon there are men with nets on the valley road.

events.text: The painter comes back the next year and the year after, and on the third year you come up to the stool at dusk and speak. {npc} does not drop the brush this time. {He} only says, "The hooves. The old books say a horse's. The drawing in the palace says a deer's. Which?" and holds the brush over the silk and waits.

choices.text: "A horse's hooves, a deer's body. And paint the grass under them standing"

mem.note: told me how to paint your feet

effects.log: {npc} paints the grass first, every blade upright under the hooves, and then the beast above it. "So the heir sees what it is for," {he} says, and you did not have to explain.

choices.text: "Make the horn small. No heir should think it is a weapon"

mem.note: asked me to paint your horn small

effects.log: The horn on the banner is so small that the chief painter sends it back twice. {npc} sends it up a third time unchanged, with a note that says the beast insisted. Nobody at court asks which beast.

choices.text: "Paint what you see. I will stand still"

mem.note: stood for me all night

effects.log: You stand by the lamp until the oil runs out. {npc} paints the scales one by one and gets the colours wrong where your coat is still grey, and asks why, and you tell {him} about the ribbons. {He} leaves those patches grey on the silk.

events.text: The investiture. From the ridge above the palace road you watch the heir's procession go by: the parasols, the fans, the drums, twenty-two kinds of regalia, and in the middle of them a yellow banner on a bamboo pole three times a man's height. One bearer holds the pole with its butt set in a cup at the waist; two more walk beside on the cords, keeping it steady in the wind. On the banner, you. The heir, in the palanquin behind it, cannot stop looking up at it.

choices.text: Follow the procession along the ridge, unseen, all the way to the gate

effects.log: You keep pace with your own picture for half a day. When the procession turns in at the palace gate the banner dips, as banners do at a gate, and you find you have dipped your head too.

choices.text: Stand on the ridge in full sight for one moment, so the heir looks up from the banner to the hill

effects.log: The heir looks from the banner to the ridge, and back, and back again. You are gone. For the rest of a long life the heir will tell people that the banner breathed.

choices.text: Watch the crowd, not the banner

effects.log: A row of grooms in a lord's colours, looking up at the banner the way a buyer looks at a horse. A boy on his father's shoulders, looking at it the way you would want. You remember both faces.

events.text: Decades on. Between processions the banner lives in a storehouse of the Office of Regalia, rolled on its pole and wrapped in blue cotton. A family of rats has found the wrapping warm and the paste in the silk delicious. The old storekeeper has asked for a cat. The request is with the Board of Rites, where it will be for some years.

choices.text: Sit in the storehouse through the winter. The rats will move, or they will not

effects.log: They do not move. They come and sleep against your flank, because nothing living is afraid of you, and eat less of the banner because they are warm. In spring the storekeeper finds seven fat rats, one beast-shaped warm place in the dust, and a banner only slightly chewed.

choices.text: Lay a road of windfall chestnuts from the storehouse to the barn across the yard

effects.log: It takes three nights and a great many chestnuts. By the fourth the rats live in the barn and think it was their idea. The storekeeper never gets the cat and puts it down to prayer.

choices.text: Ring the bell voice once in the storehouse and send them running into the snow (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: One word, and the rats go out into the frozen yard in a grey rush. Two of them do not get as far as the barn. The banner is safe. You stand over the two small shapes in the snow until the storekeeper comes with a lamp. (Bent +1)

events.text: A new king, and a vain one. The order goes out from the palace: the qilin banner will be carried in the king's own procession from now on, at the front, "since heaven's beast plainly favours the throne". The heir is twelve and is not consulted. The old bearers, who have carried that banner for the heir's line for decades, are said to be very quiet about it.

choices.text: Stand in the palace road in front of the king's procession, very still, until it stops

effects.log: The drums stop. The parasols stop. The king leans out of the palanquin and you look at the king, and then at the banner, and then at the heir's small palanquin far behind. Nobody speaks. In the morning the banner is back with the heir, and the king says it was always meant to be.

choices.text: Go to the old bearers at night and speak with them

effects.log: The three old bearers listen on the storehouse step. On the morning of the procession the banner's cords break, both of them, at the palace gate, and it cannot be carried. It is carried with the heir the next month, and the cords hold fine.

choices.text: Let it be. It is silk on a pole; the beast is up here

effects.log: The king walks behind your picture for years and the reign goes as it would have gone. The heir grows up seeing the banner go by in front of someone else, and learns what that is like. Perhaps that is a lesson too.

events.text: A new law: the grand princes, the king's sons by the queen, are to wear a square badge over the heart, woven in gold thread, and the beast on it is to be the qilin. In a weavers' quarter of the capital a master weaver has the commission and no idea what a qilin looks like, and the gold thread is very expensive to get wrong.

choices.text: Stand in the weaver's courtyard one night under the moon

effects.log: The weaver comes out for water and stands with the bucket for a long time. Then goes in and works until dawn. The badge that goes up to the palace has your face on it, rather startled.

choices.text: Leave a banner painter's sketch on the weaver's step

effects.log: You borrow a sketch from the Office of Painting, which will not miss it for a month, and leave it weighted with a stone on the step. The badge is woven from it: a beast on standing grass.

choices.text: Stay away. You do not want to be worn

effects.log: The weaver makes it up from a lion, a dragon and a deer, and it is not bad. The grand princes wear it. You find you mind more than you thought you would.

events.text: The old king is dead and the new one is a boy of eleven. Among the boy's uncles, the grand princes, one is clever, well loved and impatient, and the swordsmen of the capital have begun to find their way to that one's gate at night. {npc} wears you over the heart in gold. You come into the garden behind the house in the dark, and the grand prince sees the badge and the beast at the same time, and laughs, not unkindly.

choices.text: "The badge is a beast that waits. Do you know why they chose it?"

mem.note: came off my badge to tell me to wait

ok.log: {npc} stops laughing. "Because it does not tread on the grass," {he} says. "Even the grass that is in its way." {He} sends the swordsmen home that night, and they are angry, and you stay in the garden until the last one has gone.

mem.note: told me to wait

fail.log: "Because it is pretty," {npc} says, "and harmless, and so are the princes who wear it. Not this one." {He} goes in. The swordsmen keep coming.

choices.text: Say nothing. Stand on the lawn until {npc} looks at the grass under your hooves

mem.note: stood by me, and the grass under you did not bend

effects.log: It takes most of the night. Near dawn {npc} kneels and runs a hand over the lawn where you stood, and it is not even damp. {He} does not say anything either. That is how you know it worked a little.

choices.text: "Wear something else, then. I am not your permission"

mem.note: would not be my banner

effects.log: "I did not ask you," {npc} says, "and I do not need you. I need the people to think I have you." {He} touches the gold beast over the heart. "Which they do."

events.text: Three years later, the night it was always going to be. The grand prince's gate opens at the second watch and the swordsmen come out in a line, with {npc} at their head in a plain robe and the gold badge over the heart. The road to the boy king's palace runs past the lane where you are standing.

choices.text: Stand in the middle of the lane and let them come to you

ok.log: {npc} stops a sword's length from you. The swordsmen behind stop. For a long time nobody moves, and then {npc} unpins the badge, looks at it in the moonlight, and pins it back, and turns the whole line round. The boy king never knows how near it came.

fail.log: {npc} looks at you and walks round you, and the swordsmen follow, every one of them careful not to touch you. By morning there is a new king. The boy is sent to a far province and does not live long there. You did not harm anyone. You stood in the lane all night, and it was not enough. (-12 health: the cold of a whole night in the lane)

choices.text: Go to the boy king's palace first and stand on the roof of the gate, in sight of the guards

effects.log: The palace guards see the beast of the heir's banner on their gate roof and turn out to a man, and are all on the wall when the grand prince's swordsmen come up the road. Nobody fights. Everybody goes home. The grand prince is sent to a far province, alive.

choices.text: It is not your throne and not your vow's business. Stay in the lane, out of the road

effects.log: They pass the end of the lane without seeing you. By morning there is a new king with your gold beast over the heart. The new reign is not a bad one. You learn, in time, to stop listening for the boy's name.

events.text: {npc} is old and dying, in a great house or a far province, and has asked to be buried in the robe with the gold badge over the heart. You come to the window on the last night. {He} knows the sound of you.

choices.text: Stand at the window until it is over

effects.npcPass: old age, in the robe with the gold badge
effects.log: "You were right, or you were wrong," {npc} says to the window, "and I have never been sure which." Near dawn {he} stops talking. They bury {him} in the robe. Under the earth the gold thread keeps your shape long after the silk has rotted.

choices.text: Speak once, in the bell voice, so softly the watchers think it is the wind

effects.npcPass: old age, listening to a bell
effects.log: One sentence. What it is, only {npc} hears. {He} smiles at the ceiling. The watchers by the bed say afterwards that a temple bell rang, very far off, though there is no temple in that valley.

choices.text: Do not go in. Some deathbeds are not yours

effects.log: {npc} dies looking at the window, which is empty. You are under the persimmon tree in the yard. You hear it all. It is the closest you can come.

events.text: The Board of Rites revises the code: from now on not only the grand princes but every prince of the blood will wear the qilin over the heart. A hundred badges are on the looms. The old weaver's granddaughter is the master of the workshop now, and on the night the gold thread arrives you feel it, the way you feel a ribbon tied: you could breathe yourself into the thread. Every prince who wore you would feel you there whenever they thought of seizing the throne. You would be that, and nothing else, for good.

choices.text: Leave one scale on the weaver's table for the pattern, and go

effects.log: The weaver keeps the scale in a lacquer box and weaves every badge from it for years. The princes wear a very good likeness. It is only thread. You find, standing on the ridge, that you are glad.

choices.text: Let thread be thread. Some of them will wait, and some will not, with or without you

effects.log: You walk back to the cave by the river road and do not look at the capital. The badges are woven. Some princes wait. Some do not. None of them, ever, are made to.

choices.text: Go into the gold thread. Be the conscience of the ones who must wait

effects.log: You stand in the workshop among the looms and breathe out, once, and do not breathe in. In the morning the weavers find no beast, only a hundred gold badges glowing a little in the dark, and a hoofprint on the threshold that will not wash off.

events.text: The child of the yellow ribbon, {npc}, is the last grandchild of a prince's line that was disgraced two reigns ago; that is why the birth was in a poor house. Now the king has no son, and a eunuch has come down from the capital with a sealed letter and a palanquin. The child is to be raised in the palace as the heir. {He} is standing in the yard with a bundle and has not cried, and is clearly going to.

choices.text: Walk beside the palanquin the whole way to the capital, unseen

mem.note: walked beside the palanquin all the way

effects.log: Nine days of road. Twice in the night you turn bandits off it without their knowing why they changed their minds. On the last morning {npc} pulls back the curtain and looks straight at the bamboo where you are and nods, as if to a servant.

choices.text: Show yourself to the escort at the crossroads, so the court knows what it is getting

effects.log: Forty men of the escort see the beast of the heir's banner at the crossroads, bowing its head to a palanquin. By the time the child reaches the palace, every servant there has been told, and nobody dares be unkind.

choices.text: Let {him} go alone. An heir must learn the road

effects.log: You watch from the ridge until the palanquin is a speck. Later you hear that {npc} cried for one day and then stopped and asked for books. That is the sage in {him}.

events.text: The old king does not die. Year after year, the heir {npc} waits: reads, attends, bows, waits. A party of ministers has begun to come to the heir's pavilion at night with cups of warm wine and long sentences about the king's health. Tonight {npc} sends them away early and walks out alone to the pine at the end of the garden, where you are, and says, "They want me to seize it. They say heaven sent you to my birth, so heaven wants me on the throne now. Does it?"

choices.text: "A throne taken has to be held. A throne waited for holds itself"

mem.note: told me to wait

effects.log: {npc} repeats it back, to have it right. Then {he} laughs, very quietly. "That is a good sentence. I will be waiting a long time, I think. I may need more of them."

choices.text: Tell the story of the grand prince who did not wait

mem.note: told me about a prince who seized the throne

effects.log: You tell it all: the lane, the swordsmen, the boy in the far province. {npc} listens without moving. At the end {he} asks only, "Was the reign bad?" "No," you say. "That is worse," {npc} says, and goes in.

choices.text: Lie down under the pine and say nothing. Let {him} sit against your flank

mem.note: lay with me under the pine

effects.log: The heir of a kingdom sits against a beast's flank under a pine and falls asleep. In the morning the ministers find {npc} there alone, very calm, and their sentences are much shorter after that.

events.text: The old king is dying at last, and too slowly for some. At the third watch the ministers' party comes to the heir's gate with torches and a hundred swords: now, tonight, before the queen's kin can move; heaven's beast was at your birth. {npc} comes out onto the step in a sleeping robe. You are in the gateway.

choices.text: Stand in the gate between them, and look at the heir

ok.log: {npc} looks at you, and at the torches past you, and says in a clear voice, "My father is still alive. Go home." Nobody goes home at once. But nobody comes through the gate. By dawn the street is empty and the old king, three halls away, sleeps on.

fail.log: {npc} looks at you a long time, and then takes the sword the captain holds out, and steps past you, not touching you, into the torchlight. "For the peace you promised," {he} says, not to you. The yellow ribbon on your horn tightens, and you know what it will do by the end of the year.

choices.text: Trust {him}. Stay in the dark of the garden and let it be the heir's own choice

ok.log: You hear it from the garden. "No," {npc} says, once, and the captain argues, and {npc} says it again exactly the same way. The torches go. You have never been prouder of anything you did not do.

fail.log: You hear the argument go on and on and then stop. The gate creaks. The torches move off toward the king's hall with the heir among them. The ribbon on your horn pulls, like a hand on a sleeve. It will tear by the year's end.

choices.text: Go out into the street and lie down across the gateway, so they must step over you to bring the heir out

effects.log: The captain kicks you, once, to see if you will move. You do not. Nobody else will be the second to kick heaven's beast. {npc} stands on the step all night above you, and at dawn says, "Thank you. Get up. They have gone." (-15 health)

events.text: The old king dies asleep in the spring. The court must name the next king, and the queen's kin have a candidate of their own, a younger prince who did not wait so prettily. {npc} has waited most of a lifetime for this morning and is standing in the outer court with the other princes in mourning hemp, with no expression at all.

choices.text: Come down into the throne yard at the hour of the naming, and stand beside {npc}

mem.note: stood beside me in the throne yard

effects.log: The whole court sees the beast of the heir's banner walk across the flagstones and stand beside one prince in mourning hemp. There is no debate. {npc} is crowned in the autumn and reigns as {he} waited: carefully, without hurry, and without one execution.

choices.text: Tell {him} in the night: let the younger one have it, and teach the reign from outside

mem.note: told me to step aside

effects.log: {npc} steps aside before the court can choose. The younger prince is crowned and is a frightened, unkind king who listens, in the end, only to the old uncrowned heir in the pavilion at the end of the garden. It is a strange kind of reign. It holds.

choices.text: Stay away. Let the court choose without an omen in the yard

ok.log: The court chooses {npc} by one voice. Nobody can say afterwards whose. {npc} is crowned in the autumn, and in the first week of the reign has the qilin banner moved from the storehouse to the throne hall, where it is aired every spring.

fail.log: The court chooses the younger prince. {npc} bows to the new king first of all the princes, and goes home to the pavilion and the books, and lives to be very old and never once speaks of it. Students come. More students than the king has ministers.

events.text: A servant in a stained travelling coat comes to the cave mouth and kneels on the stone and does not know whom to address, so addresses the cave. {npc}, the heir of the yellow ribbon, is dying, and has asked for the window to be left open on the side facing your mountain. That is the whole message. The servant has walked eleven days to give it.

choices.text: Go at once. (The Last Appearance: be at the deathbed)

effects.log: You are past the servant and down the rapids before the servant has finished bowing. Go to the deathbed: the ribbon must be untied by the hand it was tied for.

choices.text: Speak to the servant first: "Tell me what the heir has done with the years"

effects.log: The servant tells you, kneeling, for an hour: the schools, the stopped executions, the flood granaries, a war not fought. Then you go. (The Last Appearance: be at the deathbed.)

choices.text: Carry the servant back with you on your back, so the message-bearer is there too

effects.log: The servant rides heaven's beast for eleven days' road in three, holding your mane and weeping and laughing in turns. (The Last Appearance: be at the deathbed.)

events.text: The yellow is in your coat now, from the belly up the flanks, the colour of old gold. They bury the heir of the yellow ribbon on a south slope, under a mound with a stone sheep and a stone official beside it. On the morning of the burial, the qilin banner is carried in the procession, in front of the coffin, which has never been done for anyone before.

choices.text: Walk behind the coffin at the end of the procession, in full sight

effects.log: Nobody turns round. Everybody knows. At the mound the banner bearers lower your picture, and you lower your head, and an old minister who was once a child in the crowd says aloud: "Both of them."

choices.text: Lie on the slope above the mound for a season, until the grass has grown back over the digging

effects.log: The grass comes back over the mound by midsummer. You have not bent a blade of it. The grave-keeper finds a hollow in the slope above, beast-shaped, and does not mow there.

choices.text: Go home. The ribbon is untied; there is nothing left to wait for

effects.log: You go back to the cave and look at the yellow in your coat in the still water below the rapids. It does not fade. That is what home means, it turns out: it does not fade.

events.text: The child of the white ribbon, {npc}, was born in a village on the edge of an old battlefield, where the plough turns up arrowheads every spring. From a small age the child talks to people in the field who are not there. The village mudang, an old shaman with a drum, has come to the house twice and sat with {him}, and the third time asks the parents for the child.

choices.text: Stand in the field at dusk where the child can see you, among the people who are not there

mem.note: stood with the dead in the field

effects.log: {npc} sees you among the dead and is not frightened of any of you after that. "They are only cold," {he} tells the mudang. "The beast said so." You did not say anything. The child is a better listener than that.

choices.text: Go to the shaman's house in the night and lie down by the drum

effects.log: The old mudang wakes, sees you, and takes up the drum and plays one slow rhythm, the one for a guest. In the morning the shaman goes to the child's parents a third time and does not have to ask.

choices.text: Leave it. The dead in that field have waited long enough for someone; the child will do

effects.log: You watch from the hill for a year. The child goes to the shaman's house with a bundle and a drum too big to carry, and drags it.

events.text: {npc} is grown and has a drum of {his} own, and white hemp, and paper streamers. The battlefield has never had its rite: too many dead, too long ago, too many sides. Tonight {npc} will hold the gut that sends the dead on, alone, in the middle of the field. The villagers have gone indoors and shut the shutters. You stand at the edge of the field, and the dead turn to look at you.

choices.text: Walk into the field and stand behind {npc}, so the dead see the two of you together

mem.note: stood behind me at the rite

effects.log: All night the drum, and the long white cloth torn in two down its length so the dead can walk the road between. Near dawn they go, a few and then many, and some of them stop to look at you, as if at something they had heard of once and not believed.

choices.text: Walk the edge of the field all night, so no living thing comes in to break the rite

effects.log: A drunk on the road, two dogs, a curious boy. Each one finds a beast in the way and goes home. The rite is not broken. In the morning {npc} sleeps on the grass where the drum stopped.

choices.text: Ring the bell voice once at the end, for the ones who will not go

effects.log: At the last there are a few who will not leave: soldiers still angry. You speak once, very low. They turn round. {npc} looks at you over the drum and nods, as at a colleague.

events.text: A demonic sect hears of a mourner who can send the dead wherever {he} likes, and wonders if {he} could send them back. Men in black come to the village and take {npc} to their hall in the hills, to raise the battlefield as an army. You cannot fight. You go to the hall anyway.

choices.text: Walk in through the front gate and lie down at the mourner's side, and do not move

ok.log: They beat you, a little, and you do not move; they try to drag you, and you are heavier than a house. On the third day the sect master, who is superstitious, has the gate opened. "Take your shaman and go." (-15 health)

fail.log: They let you lie there. They let {npc} go, in the end, because a beast of heaven at their gate is bad for their name. But first they made the mourner drink something, to make the dead come, and the dead did not, and {npc} walks out grey in the face. {He} will not live long now. (-20 health)

choices.text: Go in at night over the water of the moat and lead {him} out the way you came

effects.log: The moat holds you and the mourner beside you, step by step, while the guards on the wall shout and nobody dares shoot at heaven's beast. By dawn you are three valleys away. {npc} laughs the whole last mile, and cannot stop.

choices.text: Let the sect master see what you are, and offer yourself in the mourner's place

effects.log: The sect master takes the trade, gladly, and keeps you in a courtyard for a month, and finds out that a qilin will not do one thing it is told. On the thirtieth morning the gate is open and there is no guard, and nobody ever explains it.

choices.text: Trample the gate down and the guards with it (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: The gate goes down, and two guards under it, and you walk over them to the mourner. They will live, but not on the same legs. {npc} looks at you all the way home and says nothing at all. (Bent +3)

events.text: {npc} wants to die on the battlefield, among the cairns the village has piled where the dead were sent. The villagers carry the mourner out on a door and set it down by the biggest cairn, and leave the white drum beside it, and go back to the edge of the field. Every one of them is looking at the hill where you usually stand.

choices.text: Go down. (The Last Appearance: be at the deathbed)

effects.log: You come down off the hill in front of the whole village. Go to the deathbed: the white ribbon is waiting to be untied.

choices.text: Bring a stone from the rapids for the cairn on your way

effects.log: A white river stone, carried in your mouth for three days. You set it on the cairn. {npc} sees it and laughs, weakly, the same laugh as the moat. (The Last Appearance: be at the deathbed.)

choices.text: Sit on the hill and let the village have the first hours with {him}

effects.log: You wait until the drum has gone quiet and the villagers have said what they have to say. Then you go down. (The Last Appearance: be at the deathbed.)

events.text: White comes into your coat: the mane, the beard, the tuft of the tail, the white of a mourning robe. In the village by the old battlefield the plough still turns up arrowheads, but nobody hears anything in the field at night any more. The children have started to play there.

choices.text: Add a stone to every cairn on the field, one a night, all winter

effects.log: Ninety-one cairns. Ninety-one nights. The village takes it up the next winter without being asked, and keeps it up for generations, a stone a year, and no one remembers who began it.

choices.text: Lie in the field where the children play and let them climb on you

effects.log: The children are not afraid at all. The parents are terrified for about a day and then bring their own lunches. You lie there all spring with your white mane full of grass seed.

choices.text: Go home and look at the white in the still water

effects.log: White, the colour of mourning, in a coat that is meant to be a sign of peace. You understand the mourner better now than you did while the mourner was alive, which is the way of these things.

events.text: You wake in the cave with light round your legs. Pale fire, the colour of the inside of a shell, curling up from your hooves to your knees and down again like breath. The straw under you is not even warm. You stand very still for a long time, because the meadow outside is dry this year, and you do not trust anything new.

choices.text: Walk out onto the dry meadow, one hoof at a time, and look behind you

effects.log: Nothing. Not a scorch, not a curl of smoke. A grasshopper walks through the flame round your left foreleg and out the other side and goes on with its day. The fire is yours and it burns nothing. It took you most of the morning to believe it.

choices.text: Stand in the rapids until it goes out

effects.log: It does not go out. It burns under the water, pale, and the fish come to look at it. You stand there a whole day, cold to the bone, and come out with the fire exactly as it was. (-5 health)

choices.text: Go up to the temple at night and let the monks see

effects.log: The night monk sees fire on the temple steps and runs for water, and then sees what is burning, and puts the bucket down very carefully, and bows to it.

events.text: A village is burning in the valley below the ridge: a cooking fire in a dry wind, one thatch roof and then the next. People are coming out with buckets and going back for children. A grandmother is standing in the lane shouting a name at a house that has no door left.

choices.text: Walk into the house

effects.log: The fire round your legs meets the fire of the house and the two do not know what to make of each other. You come out of the smoke with a child of four asleep on your back, and where your hooves went through the burning room there is a path of straw that did not catch. (-10 health)

choices.text: Walk the line between the burning houses and the standing ones, back and forth, all night

effects.log: Wherever you walk, nothing burns: not the thatch you brush, not the fence. By dawn half the village is ash and half of it stands, and between them is a line of hoofprints that is not even black. (-8 health)

choices.text: Show the villagers where the stream can be turned, with your horn in the soft bank (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: The stream comes over its bank where you gouge it and runs down the lane and the fire dies in it. It also drowns a meadow full of nesting larks. You count them in the morning. (Bent +1)

events.text: In the market town, the omen-readers have a new tale: a beast with burning legs was seen in the village the night it burned. Half the town says it put the fire out. The other half says it lit it. A preacher with a bell is saying the second thing very loudly on the bridge, and has a crowd.

choices.text: Walk across the bridge at noon, through the crowd, burning, and let them watch the planks

effects.log: The planks do not char. A small child holds a hand in the flame round your foreleg and says, "It is cold!" in a voice that carries to the whole bridge. The preacher has a bad afternoon.

choices.text: Go to the burned village and help rebuild, by night, so the answer is there in the morning

effects.log: Roof beams carried down from the ridge, stones for walls. By spring the village has new houses and nobody has seen who built them, and the bridge preacher has nothing to say that anyone wants to hear.

choices.text: Let them argue. An omen is what people make of it

effects.log: They argue for a generation. In the end there are two shrines, one on each side of the river: one to the beast that brought the fire, one to the beast that put it out. Both get offerings of chestnuts. You eat from both.

events.text: A white moth flies into the fire round your foreleg one summer night and does not come out. It is sitting there, inside the flame, opening and closing its wings. The next night it is still there. It has decided, apparently, that this is a good place to live.

choices.text: Keep very still at night so the moth can sleep

effects.log: All summer you sleep standing with one foreleg out, like a heron. The moth lives in the flame until the first frost, which is much longer than a moth lives. You decide not to think too hard about why.

choices.text: Walk on as usual. It chose; it can choose again

effects.log: The moth rides your foreleg up mountains and over rivers for a season, and leaves one evening for a lamp in a scholar's window. You hope it was a good lamp.

choices.text: Show the moth to a child in the next village

effects.log: A child crouches by your hoof and looks at a moth sitting in fire, and you can see a whole life turning a little in that face. Somebody will be a scholar because of this. Or a fireworks maker.

events.text: Two armies have come to a plain by the river: the king's on the east bank road, a rebel duke's on the west. They have been drawing up for three days. The farmers of the plain have gone, all but a few who would not leave their barley. Everyone on both sides says the battle will be the day after tomorrow.

choices.text: Walk out into the middle of the plain at dawn, and stand

effects.log: You go out through the barley, where the farmers watch you pass with their mouths open, and into the open grass between the lines. Both armies see you at the same moment. You hear it: twenty thousand people going quiet.

choices.text: Go first to the farmers who would not leave, and lead them out over the river

effects.log: Eleven households, an ox, two pigs and a great deal of barley in sacks. You walk them over the ford in the dark. Then you go back to the plain and out into the grass between the lines. The armies have not moved.

choices.text: Watch from the ridge for a day first. Learn which general is afraid

effects.log: The king's general rides the line every hour. The duke's general sits in a tent and does not come out. One of them is afraid of losing. One is afraid of winning. You think you know which. On the second morning you walk down into the middle.

choices.text: This is not a war you can stop. Go home

effects.log: You go home. The battle is fought. In the spring the farmers come back to a plain full of mounds and plant their barley round them.

events.text: The first day. You stand in the grass between the armies from dawn. Scouts ride out from both sides, look at you, and ride back. At noon a line of archers on the east side draws, on someone's order, and holds, and holds, and their arms begin to shake.

choices.text: Stand still. Do not even turn your head

effects.log: The order to loose never comes. One by one the archers lower their bows because their arms will not hold any longer, and none of them will be the first to shoot heaven's beast. By evening nobody on the east bank is looking at the other army at all. (-5 health)

choices.text: Lie down in the grass, the way a deer does at noon

effects.log: You lie down. Twenty thousand people look at a beast taking a nap between their armies. On the west side, somebody laughs, and is shushed, and somebody on the east side laughs back. That is a thing you can work with.

choices.text: Speak once, in the bell voice, so both lines hear

ok.log: One sentence, about barley. It carries across the whole plain. On both sides, soldiers who were farmers last year look at the barley and do not look at each other.

fail.log: The sentence carries, and a young officer on the west side answers it with an arrow that takes you in the shoulder. You do not move. It is a long afternoon. (-8 health)

events.text: The night. Fires on both sides of the plain, and in the dark grass between them a conscript from the west side comes crawling out to you on hands and knees: {npc}, a farmer's child with a spear {he} does not know how to hold. "Are you real?" {npc} whispers. "If you are real, the war is wrong. Is it wrong?"

choices.text: "Yes"

mem.note: said the war was wrong

effects.log: {npc} goes back to the fires with that word, and tells it, and by morning a whole company on the west side is sitting on its shields and will not get up. One word goes a long way in an army that does not want to be there.

choices.text: "Go home. Take the spear; it will make a good bean pole"

mem.note: sent me home

effects.log: {npc} goes the other way, east and then north, round the end of both armies and home. There are a great many beans on that farm in later years, up a very straight pole.

choices.text: Let {him} lie against your flank until morning and say nothing

mem.note: slept against the qilin between the armies

effects.log: In the morning both armies see a beast in the grass with a conscript of the west asleep against it, and nobody shoots at either of them, and that is perhaps the best argument you have made yet.

events.text: The second day. The generals have had enough. At noon the drums start on both sides, and banners go up, and the lines begin to move. Your streak of unbent years is the only thing you have brought with you onto this plain.

choices.text: Stand, and look at the king's general, whose banner is nearest

ok.log: The king's general looks at you over a hundred paces of grass, and lowers the banner. Then they all do, all along the line, east and west. Nobody can say afterwards who lowered first. By evening both armies are sitting in the grass, and the farmers are coming back over the ford for their barley.

fail.log: The general looks at you, and looks away, and gives the order. Across the plain the duke's cavalry is mounting.

choices.text: Stand, with sixty years of grass behind you, and let them see it

effects.log: Something in the way you stand makes both armies go quiet at once, as a room goes quiet when someone very old comes in. The drums stop by themselves. The generals meet in the grass beside you that evening, on foot, and you stand between them while they talk.

choices.text: Walk away. You have done what you can; the rest is theirs

effects.log: You go back to the ridge. The battle is fought in the afternoon. It is not a large battle, as battles go. You count the fires on the plain that night, the funeral ones, and do not stop until there are no more.

events.text: The duke's cavalry comes across the plain at a walk and then a trot and then the ground shakes. They are coming straight at you, because you are in the middle, because the middle is where the king's line is thinnest. You can see the riders' faces now. Some of them are shouting at you to move.

choices.text: Bear it on your feet: let them ride round you and over you, and stand up again

effects.log: They ride round you and some of them over you, and you are down, and you are up again, bleeding, in the dust behind the charge, with the sun on your horn. The charge does not reach the king's line. The riders have all turned in their saddles to look back. (-30 health)

choices.text: Run before the charge and draw it off across the plain, away from the lines

effects.log: You run, and a thousand riders follow heaven's beast because nobody told them not to. You lead them across the plain and through the ford and two valleys on, and by the time they give up the battle has gone out of everyone.

choices.text: Lower your horn at the first rider (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: The first rider's horse turns from the horn and goes down, and the rider with it, and the charge breaks round you in a mess of hooves. The rider gets up, limping. You saw the leg. (Bent +3)

choices.text: Do not move

effects.log: You do not move. The first riders go round you, and the next, and then there are too many to go round. When the dust settles there is no battle: both lines have stopped, horrified, and are standing in the grass looking at the place where you were. The field is never mown again. No army will ever cross it. The two kings make peace on its edge, the next spring, without quite knowing why.

events.text: The peace is made at the edge of the plain, in a tent that is half one army's and half the other's because neither would go into the other's. Afterwards the generals walk out into the grass where you stood. It has grown back. They do not have the words for what they are looking for, so they look at the grass.

choices.text: Stand where you stood, and let the farmers mark it

effects.log: The farmers set four stones round the place. They never mow inside them. In time, nobody remembers what the stones are for, only that you do not take an army across that field, ever.

choices.text: Go and find the farmers' barley and help them bring it in

effects.log: The barley is late and half of it is down, but it is a harvest. The farmers bake you a cake of it, which you eat, and a cake for the generals, which they eat standing up, looking embarrassed.

choices.text: Leave before anyone thanks you

effects.log: You are on the ridge before the ink is dry. Thanks would make it yours, and it is not yours. It is the farmers' and the generals' and the conscript with the bean pole's.

events.text: A letter, carried by a student to the cave mouth and left under a stone: {npc}, the teacher of the blue ribbon, now has three thousand students and a name in nine provinces. And a plan. The age is cruel, the letter says; the qilin cannot come into it; so the students will make an age the qilin can come into. An army of the righteous, under your sign. The letter is very well written. It asks your blessing.

choices.text: Go to the teacher at once

effects.log: You go that night. You know what the letter is. You have seen it in other hands. You have never seen it in the hand of someone whose birth you stood at.

choices.text: Send no answer. A sage must hear silence too

effects.log: You send nothing. The students take your silence for consent, as students will. By autumn there are banners.

events.text: {npc}, the heir of the yellow ribbon, has waited a lifetime, and the age has only got worse. Now a general and half the court have come to {him} with an army and an argument: the qilin was at your birth; heaven wants you on the throne; the peace it promised needs a sword to clear the ground for it. The banners are already painted. You are on them.

choices.text: Go to the heir at once

effects.log: You go that night, past the guards, who kneel. The heir is in the garden under the pine, alone, and says without turning round, "I knew you would come. I was hoping you would not."

choices.text: Wait to see what the heir decides alone

effects.log: You wait. The heir waits too, for a sign, and you have decided not to be one. The general takes the waiting for a yes.

events.text: The camp. Yellow banners with your picture on them, a hundred of them, over ten thousand soldiers who believe that heaven's beast of peace marches with them. {npc} walks the lines in a plain robe and the soldiers touch {his} sleeve as {he} goes by. Nobody has noticed you yet, at the edge of the camp, by the horse lines.

choices.text: Walk into the middle of the camp and stand under your own banner

effects.log: The soldiers see you and cheer, because they think you have come. You stand under the banner and do not move and do not answer the cheering, and after a while it stops, and they begin to look at each other.

choices.text: Go to the horse lines and talk to the grooms and the cooks, who are not cheering

effects.log: The grooms and the cooks have been to wars before. They tell you what this army will do to the first town that shuts its gates. You knew. Now you know the town's name.

choices.text: Pull the nearest banner down with your teeth

effects.log: The silk comes down in the mud. Nobody stops you. Nobody puts it back up, either, for a long time, until an officer does it, looking over a shoulder.

events.text: The night before the march. {npc} comes out to you alone, past the sentries, and sits on a stone. "Tell me I am wrong," {he} says. "Then tell me what else to do. I have waited and worked all my life and the age is worse. You came to my birth. What was it for, if not this?"

choices.text: "It was for you to be the one who does not"

mem.note: said I was born to be the one who does not

ok.log: {npc} sits with that until the sky goes grey. Then {he} walks back into the camp and orders the banners taken down and burned, and the army sent home, and is called a coward in nine provinces, and lives.

mem.note: had no answer

fail.log: "That is a sentence," {npc} says, tired. "I needed an answer." {He} goes back to the camp. At dawn the drums.

choices.text: Lie down across the camp gate. They will have to step over you to march

effects.log: They have to. At dawn ten thousand soldiers step over heaven's beast one at a time, and every one of them looks down. A thousand of them, by noon, have turned round and gone home. The rest march. (-20 health: boots, and not all of them careful)

choices.text: Say nothing. Let {him} see the grey patches in your coat where the ribbons are not home

effects.log: {npc} looks at the grey for a long time and puts a hand on your flank where the colour would be. "I will bring it home for you," {he} says, which is exactly the wrong thing, and goes.

events.text: The army of the qilin wins its first battle, and its second, and takes a town that shut its gates. {npc} is very successful. Now a cage is being built, of gilded bronze, on a wagon: they mean to carry heaven's beast at the head of the army, since it will not walk there. {npc} sends to say it is an honour. {He} sends to say the cage will never be locked.

choices.text: Let the blue ribbon go. Turn your back on the army

effects.log: You turn away. The blue ribbon on your horn goes thin as cobweb, and by the year's end it will tear. The teacher of three thousand students takes the capital in the spring.

choices.text: Let the yellow ribbon go. Turn your back on the army

effects.log: You turn away. The yellow ribbon on your horn goes thin as cobweb, and by the year's end it will tear. The heir who waited a lifetime is crowned in a burned city, and looks for you in the crowd.

choices.text: Stand in front of the army on the road to the next town, one more day

ok.log: {npc} comes to the front of the army and looks at you on the road, and gets down off the horse, and kneels in the road, and stays there. The army goes home around the two of you. It takes all day.

fail.log: The army goes round you through the fields, which is worse. You hear the next town's gates from the road. (-15 health)

choices.text: Go into the cage. If it keeps the army from burning the next town, it is worth a life

effects.log: You walk into the golden cage on the wagon, and the door is not locked, and you never walk out of it. The army of the qilin wins every war for years. The sage you heralded sits on a throne with you in a cage of gold before it, as proof of virtue. You live a long time.

events.text: {npc} has given it up, the banners and the army and the cause, and gone back to a quiet house with books, and is called a coward by the people who wanted the war and a sage by the people who did not have to fight it. Most days {he} writes, or teaches whoever comes. Some days {he} sits by the river and cannot stop shaking.

choices.text: Walk beside {him} on the bad days

effects.log: On the bad days there are hoofprints by the river beside the footprints. {npc} never sees you. {He} stops shaking sooner, and says to the neighbours that the river is good for the nerves.

choices.text: Show yourself at the door, in front of the neighbours and the pupils

effects.log: The neighbours and the pupils see the beast of the banners bow its head at the door of the coward's house. Nobody calls {npc} a coward in that province again.

choices.text: Leave {him} alone with it. Some things a sage has to carry

effects.log: You stay away. It is the hardest thing you do that decade. {npc} carries it, and teaches it, and in the end it is the best lesson {he} ever gave.

events.text: Word comes up the rivers: the banners with your picture on them fly over three provinces now. Towns open their gates to the beast of peace, and are spared, mostly. The ones that do not are not. Children in the south have a new game called the Qilin's Army, and play it with sticks.

choices.text: Go south and stand in front of every town the army comes to, one after another

effects.log: Seven towns. You stand in front of each. Four open their gates and are spared, and three keep them shut and are spared too, because the army will not march through heaven's beast twice in a month. You come home thin. (-15 health)

choices.text: Go to the children and play the game the other way: the qilin lies down in the road

effects.log: The children of one southern village are astonished to find the real beast at their game. It changes the rules. In that village, for generations, the qilin always wins by lying down.

choices.text: Go back to the cave and let the age go where it will

effects.log: You go home. The war goes on without you, under your picture. You learn that there is such a thing as being used, and that the grass can be unbent and the heart not.

events.text: Refugees on every road out of the south, and all of them saying the same name: a warlord who has sworn to put the walled city on the river to the sword, every soul, because it held out for a whole summer. The siege lines are closed. The assault is set for the dawn after the new moon. Forty thousand people are inside.

choices.text: Go to the city

effects.log: You go south against the stream of refugees, who part for you without knowing why. The new moon is nine nights off.

choices.text: Go first to the refugees on the roads, and carry the weakest to the next valley

effects.log: Two nights of carrying the old and the small. Then you turn south. The new moon is seven nights off.

choices.text: It is too far, and too late, and the vow is the vow

effects.log: You do not go. On the morning after the new moon the sky in the south is brown. You stand in the rapids for a whole day, as if the water could wash it off.

events.text: You walk into the warlord's camp at dusk, past the sentries, who lower their spears and then do not know what to do with them. {npc} is eating in the open, by a fire, and does not get up. "I know what you are," {he} says. "A beast that cannot strike. A painting. Say what you came to say."

choices.text: "Give them one more day, and let the ones who want to leave, leave"

mem.note: bought a day

ok.log: {npc} looks at you over the fire for a long time. "One day," {he} says. "Out by the north gate, with nothing in their hands. Anyone who carries a weapon dies." It is something. It is not the city.

mem.note: refused the qilin

fail.log: "No," {npc} says, and goes back to eating. "Watch, if you like. Paintings are good at watching."

choices.text: "What did they do to you?"

mem.note: asked what they did to me

effects.log: A long silence. Then {npc} tells you, about a sibling on the city wall and a hot summer and a rope. It does not change anything. It explains everything. You stay by the fire until {he} sleeps.

choices.text: Say nothing. Stand by the fire until {he} has to look at you

effects.log: {npc} finishes eating, and looks, and laughs, and does not stop laughing until it is not laughing. Then {he} goes into the tent. The assault is not called off.

events.text: The last night before the assault. Inside the walls they are digging graves in advance and burning the books. Outside, the ladders are laid out on the grass in rows. The river runs past the east wall, deep and black, and nobody is guarding the water because nobody can cross it.

choices.text: Walk on the river all night, bringing people out along the water a few at a time

effects.log: Children first, then the old, then anyone. They walk on the river behind you, holding each other's sleeves, and the water holds them as it holds you. By dawn there are eleven hundred on the far bank. Forty thousand is a great many people. (-10 health)

choices.text: Stand at the main gate all night, outside it, facing the ladders

effects.log: You stand there in the dark with the city behind you and the army in front. Some of the soldiers by the ladders cannot sleep for looking at you. Some of them could never have slept anyway.

choices.text: Speak to the soldiers at the ladders in the bell voice, all night, one fire at a time

effects.log: Fire after fire. Some of them listen. A few hundred are gone by dawn, over the hills. Forty thousand inside, a few hundred gone outside. You do the sums and walk to the gate.

events.text: Dawn. The drums. The ladders go up and the army starts across the grass. {npc} rides at its head and passes you within a horse's length, and you see the whole thing plainly: one blow of your horn, unsheathed, here, now, and the warlord falls and the army stops, and the city lives. There is no other way left. There is no time left to look for one.

choices.text: Stand in the breach of the gate, and bear whatever comes

effects.log: They come round you and over the walls. You stand in the gate all day with the city falling behind you and do not strike, and at evening the warlord, passing, stops, and calls off the killing with half the city still alive, and nobody ever knows why. Half. (-30 health)

choices.text: Stand in the breach with thirty years of unbent grass behind you

ok.log: The army reaches the gate and stops in front of you, because the front rank stops, because it cannot do otherwise. {npc} rides up, raging, and stops too. You do not know what they see. They lower the ladders. The city lives, and you have harmed nothing.

fail.log: Thirty years were not enough. The army goes round you. You stand in the gate all day and at evening the warlord calls off the killing with half the city still alive. (-25 health)

choices.text: Strike once, for a city (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You strike once. The warlord falls, and the army stops, and does not know what to do, and goes home. Forty thousand people live. In the afternoon heaven takes your horn and your five colours and your fire, and you are a plain roe deer in the hills, and you live a long time, remembering that you were something else.

events.text: Years later you go back to the city on the river. The walls are mended. In the square there is a small shrine to a beast that stood in the gate, and in it someone has put an offering of chestnuts and a child's drawing of you with your horn very large and very sharp. That is how they remember it.

choices.text: Eat the chestnuts and leave the drawing

effects.log: The chestnuts are good. The drawing is wrong. You leave it, because the child who drew it was there, and you were not inside the walls that day.

choices.text: Stand in the square at dawn so they can see the horn is soft

effects.log: An old woman who was a girl in the siege comes and looks at the tip of your horn and touches it. "Soft," she says. "I told them. Nobody believes me." Now they do.

choices.text: Find the graves of the ones who died, and stand among them

effects.log: Outside the east wall, a long field of mounds. You stand among them a whole night. It was not your harm. It is your grief. The vow has room for that.

events.text: A king of the eastern kingdom on the sea is dying, and his tomb is already being dug: a wooden chamber under a great mound of river stones and earth. For the king's horse, a saddle, and for the saddle two mudguard flaps of white birch bark, layered and stitched flat, which want a painting of the horse that will carry the king up to heaven. The painter who has the work has never seen a heavenly horse, and has been sitting by a mountain spring for a week, waiting for one.

choices.text: Come down to the spring to drink at dusk, white with the evening light on you

effects.log: The painter goes very still among the reeds. You drink. When you look up the painter is mouthing a word, and the word is horse. You have been called worse.

choices.text: Leave a print of your hoof in the clay by the spring, and go

effects.log: The painter finds it in the morning and kneels by it for an hour and then, very carefully, takes the whole lump of clay home wrapped in a sleeve.

choices.text: Let the painter wait. Kings can be carried up by a horse

effects.log: The painter waits a month and paints a good, ordinary horse, and the king is buried with it. You feel, obscurely, that you have missed something funny.

events.text: The painter, {npc}, comes back to the spring with a lamp, bark panels and pots of red and black. When you come out of the reeds {he} does not run. {He} says, "You are not a horse." You agree. "Will you stand for one anyway? I have nine days and a king."

choices.text: "Yes"

mem.note: stood for my horse, though you were no horse

effects.log: {npc} bows to you, quickly, the way you bow to a colleague who has agreed to cover a shift, and sets out the brushes.

choices.text: "Yes. But paint the horn; it is the truth"

mem.note: asked me to paint the horn

effects.log: "A horse with a horn," {npc} says. "The court will have opinions." {He} writes it on the back of a panel, so as not to forget, and sets out the brushes.

choices.text: "No. Paint your horse. I am not one"

effects.log: {npc} nods and paints a horse from memory, and asks you to stay anyway while {he} works, for company. You stay. The horse is better for it. You do not know why.

events.text: Nine nights of standing by the spring while {npc} paints, by lamplight, on bark that drinks the colour. White body, legs reaching out in a gallop you have never in your life done, a red border of honeysuckle. On the seventh night {npc} stops over your forehead with the brush in the air and looks at the horn for a long time. "I need to know what to call it," {he} says.

choices.text: Tuck the horn down into your mane so it looks like a crescent tuft

effects.log: {npc} paints a crescent. Centuries from now scholars will argue over it in a museum, with photographs. You can feel that, somehow, the way you feel weather. You find it very funny.

choices.text: "It is a horn. Paint it as a horn"

effects.log: {npc} paints it as a horn, and the court painter-in-chief paints over it as a tuft of mane, because a heavenly horse does not have horns. Under the mane, if anyone ever looks, the horn is still there.

choices.text: "Call it what you like. You are the painter"

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it for a whole night and paints something halfway between, and says, "Let them argue." You like this painter very much.

events.text: The king's funeral. The saddle goes into the wooden chamber with the crown and the belt and the gold, and then the river stones go on top of it, thousands of them, cartload after cartload, and then the earth, until the mound is a hill. {npc} stands at the back of the crowd with paint still under {his} nails, watching the dark go down over the birch bark.

choices.text: Stand on the next hill so the painter can see you there at the end

effects.log: {npc} looks up from the mound and finds you on the hill and laughs out loud at a funeral, and has to pretend it was a sob.

choices.text: Walk round the mound three times at night, the way the mourners do

effects.log: Three times round, in the dark, while the guards sleep. Inside the hill a painted beast that is not a horse lies on a saddle for a king who did not know the difference. You feel it in there, a little, the way you feel your own reflection.

choices.text: Go home. It is a horse now. Let it be one

effects.log: You go home. For a long time afterwards, when the light is right, you catch yourself checking your reflection for a mane.

events.text: Long years after, you pass the mound. It is a grassy hill now among other grassy hills, and nobody remembers which king is in which. But you can feel the painting under there, very clearly, like a door left ajar. You could go in. Sleep on the birch bark as a white horse with a crescent on its forehead, until one day someone digs down through the stones and lifts you into the light and argues about you.

choices.text: Leave one hair from your tail in the grass on the mound, and go on

effects.log: One white hair, in the grass. It is blown away by noon. The painting under the hill does not need you to be a horse. It already knows.

choices.text: Walk on, laughing to yourself all the way to the river

effects.log: A heavenly horse. You. You are still laughing at the ford, and the ferryman looks at you very oddly, and you do not explain.

choices.text: Go in. Be the heavenly horse, and never tell

effects.log: You lie down on the side of the mound and go in through the stones and the earth and the dark, into the bark, into the gallop. Many centuries later a lamp comes down through the chamber roof, and a scholar holds you up to it, and frowns at your forehead. You never tell.

events.text: One morning you go down to drink at the rapids, and step forward to reach the deep water, and the water holds. Your hoof is on it, not in it. A ring of ripples goes out from it across the pool and comes back. You stand there on three legs on the bank and one on the river, not breathing.

choices.text: Walk out to the middle of the pool

effects.log: Four hooves on the water. The fish come up underneath to look at you, as if you were a leaf. Nothing under you is crushed. Nothing under you could be. You stand in the middle of the pool until the sun is high, learning what that means.

choices.text: Go up the rapids, on the white water itself

effects.log: You climb the White Silver Rapids on the white water, from rock to rock without touching a rock, and come out at the top soaked to the belly with spray and laughing in a way you did not know you could.

choices.text: Step back onto the bank and think about it for a season

effects.log: You think about it for a season. Then one evening you walk across the river without deciding to, because the meadow on the far side had dew on it, and the water held, because it does now.

events.text: The ferryman at the ford below the temple, {npc}, has seen you walk across the river six times this year and has stopped pretending not to. This morning {he} is sitting in the empty boat, looking at you on the far bank, and says, "If everyone could do that, I would be out of a living."

choices.text: Get into the boat and be ferried across, properly

mem.note: ferried heaven's beast across, though it could walk

effects.log: The boat goes very low in the water. {npc} poles you across with enormous dignity and refuses the fare, which you did not have, and tells every passenger for the rest of {his} life.

choices.text: "Nobody else can. Only nobody else needs to be on the water when they cross"

effects.log: {npc} thinks about that, and agrees, and goes back to work, and on flood days, when the boat cannot go, you are at the ford in the morning, and {he} walks beside you across with a rope round your neck for the passengers to hold.

choices.text: Walk off down the river, on it

effects.log: {npc} watches you go downstream on the water for a whole bend, and then picks up the pole, shaking {his} head. "Showing off," you hear, across the water.

events.text: Rice-planting time, and the valley is a sheet of water with green seedlings standing in rows. You have always gone round the paddies on the dykes, at a crawl. This spring you could walk straight across. A farmer's whole family is planting at the near end, bent double, and they have seen you on the dyke.

choices.text: Walk across the paddy on the water, between the rows, touching nothing

effects.log: Not a seedling bent. The family straightens up all together to watch. The grandmother says it is a good sign for the rice, and is right, as it turns out, though that is mostly the weather.

choices.text: Go round on the dyke as you always have

effects.log: There is a difference between being able to and needing to. You go round on the dyke. The children of the family run along beside you, and the planting falls a little behind, and nobody minds.

choices.text: Stand in the paddy on the water while they plant, so the children can see

effects.log: The children plant round you, closer and closer, until the youngest puts a seedling right between your forehooves and looks up at you, daring you to step on it. You do not.

events.text: When you stand on the river, the fish gather under you. All of them, from all down the reach, as if there were something good to eat in your shadow. A fisherman upstream, {npc}, has noticed, and has a net, and a proposal: stand in the same place every morning, and nobody in the village will go hungry again.

choices.text: Refuse. Walk off the water, and keep off this reach

effects.log: "It is only fish," {npc} says. You know. You keep off that reach all the same. The fish scatter back to their own places, and the village eats as it always did, which is not badly.

choices.text: Stand there one morning, for the village, and say nothing about it again (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: The net comes up so full it tears. The village eats for a week. You stand on the river afterwards looking at the water under you, empty now, and know exactly how many there were. (Bent +1)

choices.text: Show {him} the deep pool where the big fish live by themselves, and let {him} fish as a fisher does

effects.log: It is not you catching them. It is {npc}, with a line and patience, on a pool you happen to know. You are not sure if that is a real difference. You decide, carefully, that it is.

events.text: In the north, a king's tomb is being built in the old way: a stone chamber of polished granite, under a mound. The painters are already at work on the walls by lamplight. On the east wall a blue dragon; on the west a white tiger. You know them both, or their living kin, which is the strange part. The master painter has come up to the cave to ask, very politely, whether the beast of the Four Spirits would stand for the ceiling.

choices.text: Go north with the painter

effects.log: Twenty days of road, the painter walking, you a little behind. The painter talks the whole way, about pigments, about how hard it is to make a white that stays white in the dark. You learn a great deal about white.

choices.text: Ask first who sleeps there, and whether the sleeper was good

effects.log: The painter is honest. A middling king: two wars, one famine handled well, one handled badly. "Most of them are like that," the painter says. "That is why they want the four beasts on the walls." You go north.

choices.text: Refuse. A qilin does not lie in the dark

effects.log: The painter bows and goes. The ceiling gets lotus and honeysuckle and immortals, and no qilin, and is beautiful anyway, and nobody ever knows there was meant to be one.

events.text: The chamber is cold and smells of lamp oil and wet lime. Up on the scaffold the master painter, {npc}, lies on {his} back with the brush against the granite of the ceiling stones. Below, on the walls, the blue of the dragon and the white of the tiger are still wet. "Stand where the lamp is," {npc} says, "and look up. I want you looking down."

choices.text: Stand under the lamp all night, looking up at the stone

mem.note: stood all night under the lamp for me

effects.log: All night. Your neck aches; {npc}'s arm aches. By morning there is a beast on the ceiling among the flying immortals, looking down at where the coffin will be, with your exact expression, which you had not known you had.

choices.text: Ask for the grass under your hooves to be painted standing, even on a ceiling

effects.log: {npc} laughs on the scaffold and nearly falls. "There is no grass on a ceiling," {he} says. Then {he} paints it: one blade, upright, under one hoof. Nobody will ever notice. You will know.

choices.text: Look at the walls instead. The dragon and the tiger

effects.log: The dragon is very like. The tiger is very like. Both are a little too proud, as they would be. {npc} paints you on the ceiling looking at them both, and does not ask why the beast is smiling.

events.text: The night before the sealing. The king is in the coffin on the stone platform, the lamps are lit for the last time, and the painters have gone out. You are alone in the chamber with the walls: the blue dragon on the east, the white tiger on the west, the red bird by the door, the tortoise and snake in the north, all of them very bright. And on the ceiling, you, looking down.

choices.text: Lie down by the coffin for the night

effects.log: You lie down on the cold stone by the middling king. You find you do not mind keeping a middling king company. Most people are middling. Most of them deserve a beast on the ceiling.

choices.text: Stand in the middle and look at each wall in turn, as the guardians look in

effects.log: Four walls of beasts that guard by fighting. One ceiling with a beast that guards by watching. In the lamplight you understand, for the first time, that you are not one of them, and were never meant to be, and that this is fine.

choices.text: Breathe once on your own painted image

effects.log: One breath, on the granite. The paint there will stay a little brighter than the rest for as long as the stone lasts. Someone, some day, with a lamp, will wonder why.

events.text: Dawn. The masons are at the door with the sealing stone. You can feel the ceiling the way you feel the ribbon on your horn: a place you could go into. Up among the immortals and the lotus, above the dragon and the tiger, watching one sleeper for longer than any mound will be remembered while the colour fades from all of you.

choices.text: Walk out past the masons into the morning

effects.log: The masons flatten themselves against the passage as you go by. The stone goes in behind you. On the ceiling inside, the painted beast looks down at the sleeper on its own. It does very well without you.

choices.text: Stay until the stone is in, outside, with your forehead against it

effects.log: You stand with your forehead to the sealing stone while the masons pack the earth round it, and then you go. You never come back. You never quite leave, either.

choices.text: Go into the ceiling. Watch the sleeper

effects.log: You look up, and then you are looking down. The sealing stone goes in. The lamps go out. In the dark you can see perfectly, as painted things can: the king, the dragon, the tiger, the long slow fading of the colour. You watch, and it is enough, for as long as the colour lasts.

events.text: A proclamation on every market gate in the kingdom: the king's reign is so virtuous that the qilin must surely have appeared in it; whoever brings the beast to court alive will be given a county. Under the proclamation, a drawing of you. It is not very good. The hunters who read it are.

choices.text: Go deep into the mountains for a few years

effects.log: Far up, where there is nothing to herald and nobody to see you. You go hungry, and the age goes on without you, and the hunters search the wrong valleys. It is not hiding. You tell yourself it is not hiding.

choices.text: Go on as you were. Let them try

effects.log: They try. Nets on the ridges, salt-licks laced with sleep, dogs, a very clever trap involving a mirror. You walk round all of it, mostly. You come home one evening with a net round your hind leg and a great deal of respect for the mirror.

choices.text: Show yourself in the market square under the proclamation, and walk away before the guards arrive

effects.log: A whole market sees heaven's beast stand under the king's proclamation and look at it, and look at the people, and walk away. Nobody tries to catch you. They understand what they have been shown better than the king does.

events.text: The king's men come up the valley with masons. On the cliff above the rapids, by the mouth of your cave, they cut three large characters into the rock: the Qilin Cave. Below it, a smaller inscription: that the king's ancestor raised a qilin-horse here, and the cave belongs to the royal house, and so does the beast.

choices.text: Let them carve. Rock does not own anything

effects.log: They carve, and go, and the rain gets into the letters. In time moss has the inscription. Long after, somebody will rediscover it and make a great fuss. You will still be living in the cave, which never belonged to anyone.

choices.text: Stand at the cave mouth while they work, and watch them

effects.log: The masons work very slowly, with you watching. One of them makes a mistake in the last character and does not dare correct it. The cave belongs to the royal house with one stroke missing, which is how you prefer it.

choices.text: Go up to the temple and ask the monks to cut their own words beneath

effects.log: The monks cut, very small, under the king's inscription: "and it came to the cave because no one owned it." The king's men see it a year later and do not know how to remove it without making it famous.

events.text: You walk into the palace garden at night past guards who fall to their knees, and the king, {npc}, is there by the pond, in a robe too heavy for the summer, looking at the golden cage on its platform in the hall beyond. "So you came," {npc} says. "Of course you did. My reign is very virtuous."

choices.text: "Then you have no need of a cage"

mem.note: said I had no need of a cage

ok.log: {npc} opens {his} mouth and shuts it. In the morning the proclamation is taken down from every gate. Nobody explains why. The cage is melted for the treasury, which needs it.

mem.note: defied me in my own garden

fail.log: "Guards," {npc} says, without raising {his} voice. You are over the wall before they reach the pond. The proclamation stays up. The reward is doubled.

choices.text: Stand by the pond and say nothing until {npc} has to explain the cage, aloud, to a beast

effects.log: {npc} explains for an hour: the rebels, the famine, the ministers, the need for a sign. By the end {he} is not explaining it to you. You go away and let {him} keep hearing it.

choices.text: Lie down in the golden cage of your own will, for one night only, and walk out in the morning

effects.log: The whole court comes in the morning to see the beast in the cage, and sees it stand up and walk out of a locked door as if the bars were reeds. {npc} never tries to catch you again. {He} has seen what a cage is worth.

events.text: A rumour reaches the cave by the river road: in a village two valleys west, a sage is being born tonight, and the mother has a ribbon ready. You know before you get there. The house is too clean. The mother is too calm. There are soldiers' boots under the hay in the yard.

choices.text: Walk in anyway. If there is a real child in there, it is still being born

ok.log: There is a real child, born to a real soldier's wife who was ordered to lie still and smile. You stand at the gate two nights, as you would for any birth. The soldiers in the hay, every one of them, find they cannot get up. You leave on the third morning, and nobody follows.

fail.log: The net comes down from the roof. Silk, weighted, many hands. They have you in the cart by dawn, on the road to the capital, and you have not harmed anyone, and you lie in the cart and watch the sky. (-15 health)

choices.text: Stand at the edge of the village and ring the bell voice once, so they know you know

effects.log: One word. The soldiers come out of the hay, red-faced, and stand in the yard, and the mother sits up in bed and laughs, and you go home. A trap that has been seen is only an embarrassment.

choices.text: Turn round. A false gate is not yours

effects.log: You go back the way you came. Later you hear the trap waited a month, and the soldiers went home, and the king had the captain beaten. You think about the captain a little.

events.text: The golden cage, on a stone platform before the throne. You lie in it while the court files past in the mornings and says how virtuous the reign must be. The bars are gilded bronze and too narrow for your horn. A young guard who brings your water every day has started to bring windfall chestnuts too, at some risk.

choices.text: Bear it a year. Let them look at what they have done

effects.log: A year of mornings. The court stops saying the reign is virtuous somewhere in the second season; they cannot, with you looking at them. In the spring the king has the door opened in the night and does not watch you go. (-10 health)

choices.text: Speak once to the whole court in the bell voice

ok.log: One sentence. The court goes so quiet that the king can hear it too. That afternoon the cage is opened. Nobody admits to having ordered it.

fail.log: One sentence, and the king laughs at it, and the court laughs after. You lie down again. Next year, then. (-5 health)

choices.text: Ask the young guard, quietly, to leave the latch undone one night

effects.log: The latch is undone on the night of the new moon. You are past the walls by dawn. The young guard is flogged for it and leaves the service and becomes a chestnut farmer, and is happy, and sends you, every autumn, by no road at all, a basket.

choices.text: Walk out over the palace pond, on the water, where nobody has thought to guard

effects.log: The cage is by the throne; the throne is by the window; the window is over the pond. Bars are not made for a beast that does not need the ground. You are gone across the water before the lamps are lit.

events.text: It is a hard age, and the lord of the western marches has called a great autumn hunt to show that he is not afraid of it. Beaters in a line three valleys wide, dogs, horns, the lord's banner on the ridge. They are not hunting you. They do not know what you are. They are hunting everything.

choices.text: Run for the rapids before the line closes

ok.log: You are over the white water before the dogs reach the bank. The beaters drive three valleys and find a great many deer and no idea that anything else was there.

fail.log: The line closes before the rapids. Dogs on both sides. You stand still in a thicket with the horns all round you and know you will be found. (-10 health)

choices.text: Lie still in the cave and let it pass over

effects.log: Three days in the dark of the cave with the horns going over the ridge above. On the fourth the valley is quiet and smells of blood and woodsmoke. You do not go out for a week.
