choices.text: Go out in front of the beaters and lead the deer out of the line (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: The deer follow you through a gap in the line, a whole herd, and in the rush a fawn goes down under the others and does not get up. The herd is saved. The fawn is not. The beaters have seen you now. (Bent +1)

events.text: The snare is silk, set low in the ravine where only something with very careful feet would go. It takes your foreleg, and you turn the wrong way, and you hear the bone go. Then the dogs, and the carter who set the snare, staring at you, and saying to the others, "What is it? It is not a deer. What is it?"

choices.text: Lie still and let them take you. You will not kick a dog

effects.log: They bind your legs and lift you into a cart, very carefully, because they are frightened of you. Your foreleg is wrong below the knee. You lie on the straw and look at the sky and do not kick anyone. (-20 health)

choices.text: Break the snare and run on three legs

ok.log: The silk goes, and you go, on three legs, over the ravine lip with the dogs behind and into the rapids. They never find you. Your foreleg takes a whole winter to set. (-15 health)

fail.log: The silk holds. You go down. They have you in the cart before you can stand. (-25 health)

choices.text: Kick the carter off the edge of the ravine and go (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: One kick, with the good hind leg. The carter goes over. You go the other way on three legs. You hear the sound at the bottom from a long way off and do not stop, and know you will hear it always. (Bent +10; -15 health)

events.text: The lord's courtyard, in the cart, on the straw. Men stand round you in a ring and argue. A deer with scales. A horse with a horn. An ill omen: kill it. A good omen: keep it. A monster: burn it. Nobody knows what you are. The lord wants to know by evening.

choices.text: Lie still and listen to every argument

effects.log: By evening you have heard every thing a frightened crowd can think of. Not one of them thinks of what you are. It is not their fault. You did not come in a time when you could be known.

choices.text: Speak, once, in the bell voice

effects.log: One sentence. Half the ring falls back and the other half goes for spears. The lord comes out to see what the noise is, and looks at you a long time, and says nobody is to touch it until the scholars have seen it.

choices.text: Look for one face in the crowd that knows

effects.log: There is one. At the back, by the gate, someone old, who has stopped arguing and is just looking at the ribbon on your horn.

events.text: Someone pushes through the ring: {npc}, very old now, one of the sages whose birth you heralded, in the lord's service as a scholar in this hard age because there was nowhere else. {He} sees the ribbon still tied to your horn and stops, and puts a sleeve over {his} face, and the sleeve is wet. "For whom have you come?" {npc} says. "For whom? There is no one here worth it."

choices.text: Look at {npc} until {he} understands: you came for {him}, and it was worth it

effects.log: {npc} stops weeping. Then {he} stands up in the ring and tells the lord, in a voice none of them knew {he} had, exactly what you are and what it will mean for the lord's house if you die in that yard. You are on the river road by midnight with a splinted leg.

choices.text: Ask {him}, in a whisper, to open the cart after dark

effects.log: After dark the old sage comes with a knife for the ropes and a splint and a lantern. You go out of the gate on three legs. In the morning the lord is told the beast vanished, and the old scholar is not believed, and does not care.

choices.text: Let it end here, with the ribbon on your horn and the sage weeping

effects.log: You put your head in the old sage's lap in the cart, in the lord's courtyard, among men who do not know what you are. {npc} weeps into the sleeve until it is wet through, and says that the way has come to an end, and puts down the brush, and writes no more.

events.text: An old scholar of the lord's house, {npc}, comes into the yard with the others, and does not argue. {He} looks at the faded ribbon on your horn for a long time and then covers {his} face with a sleeve and weeps, so that the hunters step back. "Who tied that?" {npc} asks nobody. "Who would have, in an age like this?"

choices.text: Lift your head and let {him} see your eyes. You are not finished

mem.note: showed me the beast in the cart was not finished

effects.log: {npc} stops weeping, and wipes the sleeve across {his} face, and turns to the lord and starts arguing for your life in long, rolling, unanswerable sentences, and does not stop until the cart is turned round and driven out of the gate.

choices.text: Wait for night and break the ropes

ok.log: The ropes go at the second watch. You go over the wall on three legs and are in the rapids by dawn. Behind you, an old scholar sits on in the empty yard and laughs, for the first time in years.

fail.log: The ropes hold. Morning. The old scholar is still there by the cart, and has not slept. On the third night {he} comes with a knife and a lantern and says nothing at all, and you go over the wall on three legs. (-10 health)

choices.text: Let it end here, with the old scholar weeping over you

effects.log: You lay your head against the cart rail by the old scholar's hand. {npc} weeps until the sleeve is wet through and says, to the lord, to the yard, to no one, that the way has come to an end. {He} writes no more after that day. You do not leave the courtyard.

events.text: Envoys from the Martial Alliance and from the unorthodox sects arrive at the cave on the same day, by different roads, and stand on opposite sides of the rapids glaring at each other. They want the same thing: a witness for a peace conference that neither side trusts the other to hold. Somebody who cannot lie and cannot be bought and will not draw a sword. They have both thought of you.

choices.text: "I will come. On one condition: no weapons in the room, not even the hidden ones"

effects.log: Both envoys agree at once and both are lying about the hidden ones. You know that. It is still a better start than most peace has.

choices.text: Come, and say nothing of conditions

effects.log: The envoys go back to their halls by their separate roads, both of them convinced the beast is on their side. That is what a witness is for, apparently.

choices.text: Refuse. Let them learn to trust each other without a beast in the room

effects.log: They do not learn. The conference is never held. The feud goes on for another generation, and you hear about it at the ford, now and then, in the form of funerals.

events.text: The pavilion by the river: two rows of mats, orthodox on the left, unorthodox on the right, every face a famous one. You lie at the head of the room where both rows can see you. A young servant, {npc}, goes along the low tables pouring tea into celadon cups, and {his} hands are shaking, and you smell it before the first cup is full: something bitter that is not tea.

choices.text: Rise, and drink the first cup yourself before anyone else can

effects.log: You walk down between the rows and put your muzzle in the sect leader's cup and drink it to the bottom, and lie down again. The whole room watches heaven's beast go grey and sweat and not die. Nobody touches their tea. The talks go much faster after that. (-25 health)

choices.text: Knock the tray out of {his} hands with your tail as {he} passes

effects.log: The tray goes over, the cups smash, the tea runs across the floor and turns the lacquer white where it touches. Sixty swords that were not in the room are in the room. Every one of them is pointing at {npc}, who is on the floor with {his} arms over {his} head.

choices.text: Ring the bell voice once: "Nobody drinks"

effects.log: Nobody drinks. Everybody looks at the servant. {npc} drops the pot and runs, and is caught in the doorway by four people from both sides of the room, which is the first thing they have done together in thirty years.

events.text: {npc} is on the floor of the pavilion with a knife at {his} throat and both sides of the murim arguing over who gets to kill {him}. Somebody in a back room paid {him}; {his} family is somewhere with someone's knife at their throats too. Everyone turns to the witness. A qilin cannot lie, they say. Say what should be done.

choices.text: Lie down over {npc}, so that nobody can reach {him} without reaching you

mem.note: heaven's beast lay down over me

effects.log: You lie down over the servant. The knives go back into sleeves. Then, because they have to do something, the two sides go looking for the back room together, and find it, and find the family, and the peace is signed in the morning over a pot of tea that the sect leaders brew themselves.

choices.text: "The hand that poured is not the hand that paid. Find the other one"

effects.log: It is the truth and they all hear it. The servant is held, not killed, and the hunt for the payer goes on all night, and the payer, when found, belongs to neither side, which surprises everyone and helps.

choices.text: Say nothing. It is their peace and their poisoner

effects.log: They wait for you to speak. You do not. Someone decides, and the knife moves, and the talks are signed anyway, over a body. You harmed no one. You leave before the ink is dry and the grass on the river road does not bend, and you wish, for once, that it would.

events.text: Years later a grown servant of the old pavilion comes to the cave mouth with a basket of chestnuts and a little child on the back. {npc} is the one who poured the tea. {He} married a carpenter. {He} has been meaning to come for a long time. {He} does not know what to say to a beast, so {he} sits on the Morning-Heaven Stone and says it all.

choices.text: Listen to all of it

effects.log: All of it. The fear, the family, the carpenter, the child. When {he} has finished the child has gone to sleep against your foreleg and {he} laughs and cries at once and you do not move until the child wakes up.

choices.text: Eat a chestnut, so {he} knows it was accepted

effects.log: You eat one chestnut. {npc} watches you do it as if it were a rite. It is, now.

choices.text: Let the child touch your horn

effects.log: The child puts a fat hand on the soft tip of your horn and squeezes it and laughs. {npc} goes white and then laughs too. That child grows up unafraid of a great many things.

events.text: A demonic cult has taken a village at the foot of your mountain. They have tied the villagers in the square, and they have sent a message up the path on a child's kite: the beast that never strikes is invited to strike. Once. Any one of us. Then the village goes free. Every day it does not, one villager does not.
events.arc: The Cult That Wants You to Kill

choices.text: Go down at once

effects.log: You go down the path in the dark. On the gate, the cult's red banners. In the square, the villagers, very quiet. On the wall, a person in black, waiting, who smiles when you come into the torchlight.

choices.text: Go down, and first send the bell voice ahead of you through the hills to the nearest town

effects.log: The bell rings in the town at midnight with no one pulling the rope. By dawn there are people on the road with lanterns, not fighters, just people, coming to see. A cult does a great deal less in front of witnesses.

events.text: The cult leader, {npc}, sits on the gate wall with legs swinging. "I want to see it," {npc} says. "Everybody says heaven's peace-beast cannot strike. I think it can. I think it just has not been asked properly. Once you have, you are a weapon like any other, and weapons can be had."
events.arc: The Cult That Wants You to Kill

choices.text: "You will wait a long time"

mem.note: would not strike

effects.log: "I have a whole village of time," {npc} says, and points at the square. You lie down in the road. So does the waiting.

choices.text: "Then I am the one you want. Let them go and keep me"

ok.log: {npc} thinks, and laughs, and agrees, because a beast is worth more than a village. The villagers are untied and go out of the gate past you, touching your flank. You walk in.

fail.log: "No," {npc} says. "I want the village and the beast. That is the whole point." Somewhere in the square, someone begins to cry.

choices.text: Look at {npc}, and ask what was done to make someone want this

effects.log: {npc} stops swinging the legs. For a moment the face goes very young. Then it closes again. "Strike me and find out," {npc} says. But not as sure, now.

events.text: The second night. One villager is already gone, and the cult has made sure you saw it. There is a way to end this now; you can feel the horn knowing it. There have to be other ways. You have until dawn to find one.
events.arc: The Cult That Wants You to Kill

choices.text: Walk round the outside of the wall all night with the pale fire high on your legs

effects.log: The cultists on the wall watch a burning beast circle the village, again and again, and the fire touches nothing, and they cannot stand it. By the third watch half of them have gone over the back wall into the dark. Fear is not harm, you tell yourself. You are almost sure.

choices.text: Go in through the river gate on the water and untie them one by one

effects.log: The river gate was left unguarded because nobody comes in by the river. Rope by rope, in the dark, with the cult asleep on the wall. By dawn the square is empty and the villagers are on the far bank with you, watching the cult wake up.

choices.text: Lie down in the gate itself, across the threshold, and wait for the people from the town

effects.log: They beat you at the gate to make you get up and fight. You do not. In the morning the townspeople come over the hill with their lanterns, hundreds of them, and the cult looks at the beast bleeding in the gate and the crowd watching, and leaves. (-15 health)

choices.text: Strike the cult leader once, and end it (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: One blow. {npc} goes down on the wall, and the cult runs, and the villagers are untied, and every one of them looks at you as they go past, and it is the look you have seen given to tigers. Somewhere a cult is very pleased. (Bent +10)

events.text: The village is free and the cult is gone. They bury the one villager who did not live, on the slope above the fields. The family asks, very carefully, whether a beast of heaven could not have saved that one too. They do not mean it as a reproach. It is one anyway.
events.arc: The Cult That Wants You to Kill

choices.text: Stand at the grave with the family, and do not explain

effects.log: You stand there through the whole burial. You do not say that a vow has a cost and this was it. They can see that. The grandmother puts her hand on your neck at the end, and leaves it there.

choices.text: Tell them the truth: you could have, by killing, and you did not

effects.log: They listen. The father goes away and does not come back for an hour. When he does, he says, "Good. Then they cannot use you." It is more than you would have said.

choices.text: Mend what you can: the houses, the gate, the fields the cult trampled

effects.log: A season of carrying beams and stones. The village is whole by harvest, except for the one grave. You go up to it every evening before you leave. (-5 health)

events.text: Plague in the market town below the ridge. Shut doors with red cloth on them, carts going out at dawn, smoke from the burning of bedding. The town has heard that a beast of heaven lives in the cave above the rapids. A delegation of three, in cloth masks, comes up to beg it to come down and make the sickness stop.

choices.text: Go down. You cannot stop it. You can be there

effects.log: You go down. The sickness does not take you, which is the only thing about you that turns out to be useful at first. You lie in the doorways of the sickhouses and the sick look at you and some of them stop being afraid.

choices.text: Tell them the truth: a qilin heralds the good and mourns the dead; it does not heal

effects.log: The three of them stand at the cave mouth a long time. Then the oldest says, "Then come and mourn," and you go.

choices.text: Stay in the cave. You are needed alive for the sages yet to be born

effects.log: You stay. The plague runs its course without you. When it is over the town does not send a delegation again. That is fair.

events.text: Among the sickhouses a young healer, {npc}, is doing the work of ten and will be dead of it in a month. {He} has been trained by someone very good; you can see it in the way {he} lays out the herbs. The medicine that would help is three days over a pass that the soldiers have closed, so the plague does not go out. Nothing can come in either.

choices.text: Carry {him} over the pass at night, and back, with the medicine

mem.note: rode heaven's beast over the closed pass

effects.log: Over the pass in the dark, past the soldiers' fires, down the far side to the herb market, and back the next night with two sacks tied to your flanks. {npc} sleeps on your back on the way home. Half the town lives that would not have. (-10 health)

choices.text: Take the healer's place in the sickhouse at night, so {he} can sleep

mem.note: watched the sick so I could sleep

effects.log: You cannot heal. You can call the healer when someone gets worse, and you do, all night, with one low note of the bell. {npc} sleeps four hours a night instead of none, and lives.

choices.text: Go to the soldiers at the pass and speak to them in the bell voice

ok.log: The captain hears you out and opens the pass for medicine, and only medicine, both ways. It is the right order and the wrong one at once, and the captain knows it, and gives it.

fail.log: The captain hears you out and keeps the pass shut, and is right to, by the books. You go back to the sickhouses with nothing.

events.text: A child in the last sickhouse is not going to live, and knows it, and is not frightened, because you are there. The child asks you whether you will come to the next life, the way you came to this one.

choices.text: "Yes"

effects.log: You do not know if it is true. A qilin cannot lie. You say it, and find you mean it, and the child closes their eyes holding your mane. You will look. In every child you herald from now on, you will look.

choices.text: Lie down so the child can sleep against you, and say nothing

effects.log: The child sleeps against your flank. Near dawn the breathing changes, and then stops, and you stay there until the healer comes, and the healer does not ask you to move.

choices.text: Ring the bell voice once, very softly, the way the temple bell sounds at dusk

effects.log: One note. The child smiles at it. The whole sickhouse hears it, and every patient in it sleeps that night for the first time in a week.

events.text: The plague ends in the spring, as plagues do, without saying why. The town counts its dead. In the square they have put up a little roofed stone, and carved on it the names, and at the top, where a guardian beast would go, a beast lying down.

choices.text: Lie down in the square beside the stone for a day, so they see it was meant

effects.log: All day the town comes past, one by one, and touches the stone and then your neck. Nobody says anything. That is the right thing to say.

choices.text: Go up to the cave. The town needs its own grief, not a beast in the middle of it

effects.log: You watch from the ridge. They do not need you. You are glad of that. You were not the cure. You were the company, and the company goes home.

choices.text: Find the young healer, and walk beside {him} for a while

effects.log: The healer is asleep on the steps of the last sickhouse, in the sun, for the first time in a year. You lie down at the foot of the steps until {he} wakes.

events.text: Something has come into the deep pool below the White Silver Rapids: something long. The fish have left. The ferry has stopped. Every night the water in the pool turns over once, slowly, the way a sleeper turns, and the village says there is an Imugi in it, a serpent waiting to become a dragon.

choices.text: Go down and stand on the pool, on the water, over it

effects.log: You stand on the water over the deep place. Below you, very far down, an eye opens. It is the size of a cartwheel and very tired.

choices.text: Go down and stand on the bank, where it can see you if it wants to

effects.log: For three nights nothing. On the fourth the water turns over and a head comes up, very slowly, and looks at you on the bank, and goes down again without a word.

choices.text: Leave it alone. Everyone is entitled to a pool

effects.log: You leave it alone. In time it leaves too, one storm night, and you never learn which way.

events.text: The serpent speaks, in a voice like gravel turning in a flood. "They say your kind cannot lie. Then look at me and tell me what I am. I have been waiting a thousand years to be told, and every monk and magistrate says what they think I want to hear."

choices.text: "A dragon that has not finished yet"

effects.log: The serpent is silent a long time. "Not finished," it says at last. "Not failed. Not finished." It goes back down into the pool. You can tell from the way the water settles that it is going to try again.

choices.text: "A serpent. That is not less than a dragon. It is a different thing"

effects.log: "Nobody has ever said that," the serpent says. You are not sure if it is pleased. You do not lie, so you do not take it back.

choices.text: "I do not know yet. Ask me again in a hundred years"

effects.log: The serpent laughs, a sound like a landslide underwater. "A hundred years," it says. "I have those." It stays in the pool a long time, and so, more or less, do you.

events.text: A storm, the worst in a generation, and from the cave mouth you watch the pool below the rapids heave up white and then something goes up out of it into the clouds: up, and up, and lost in the lightning. Afterwards there is only the pool, quiet, and the fish coming back.

choices.text: Stand on the pool where it was, in the rain, and look up

effects.log: You stand on the water in the last of the rain. Far up in the clouds, something turns, once, and looks down, you are fairly sure. Then the clouds close.

choices.text: Ring the bell voice once, up into the storm

effects.log: One note. Thunder answers it, very precisely, the same note. The temple monks write in the record that the bell rang itself in the storm, and the sky rang back.

choices.text: Go back into the cave. Whatever it became, it is its own

effects.log: You go in and lie down. The thunder goes on until dawn. In the morning there is a single scale on the stone before the cave, as long as your foreleg, still warm.

events.text: In the still water below the rapids you see it plainly, at last: the soft tip of your horn has gone thin, and under the flesh, where nothing ever showed before, there is a gleam of white. Bone. Everything you have bent is in it. You can feel the horn wanting to be what it is turning into.

choices.text: Go and find every harm you can still mend

effects.log: A field, a fawn that lived lame, a dyke. You go to each and do what you can. The gleam does not go, but it stops growing. (Bent -3; -8 health)

choices.text: Look at it a long time and do nothing yet

effects.log: It is your horn. It is the truth about you. A qilin cannot lie, and the horn is, it turns out, a qilin too.

choices.text: Rub the tip on the Morning-Heaven Stone until the white is hidden

effects.log: It hurts. It works, a little, for a little while. The flesh is pink over the white for a month. Then the white comes back. (-5 health)

events.text: Three grooms in a warlord's colours come up the valley with a saddle, a bridle of red silk and a great deal of patience. They do not try to catch you. They set the saddle on the Morning-Heaven Stone and sit down beside it and wait. A beast with a bone horn, their master says, will come to the saddle by itself in the end.

choices.text: Walk past the saddle every day, close enough to smell the leather, and never stop

effects.log: Every day. The grooms watch you pass and say nothing. It is a contest now, and both sides know it, and both sides are very polite about it.

choices.text: Kick the saddle off the stone into the rapids

effects.log: The saddle goes down the rapids and is never seen again. The grooms watch it go and then look at each other and one of them says, "He said it would want to." They go home to get another.

choices.text: Speak to the grooms, in the bell voice, about their master

effects.log: They listen. The youngest one leaves the service before the month is out. The other two stay with the saddle. Loyalty is a kind of patience too.

events.text: The warlord comes in person, {npc}, alone, without armour, and sits on the stone beside the saddle. "I do not want a peace-beast," {npc} says. "Peace-beasts are for kings who have already won. I want the one under the flesh. You know it is there. Carry me into one battle, horn first, and the armies will follow the horn, and it will be over in a day. Fewer will die than if you stay here and keep your hands clean."

choices.text: "Fewer will die by your sword, and all of them by mine"

mem.note: would not carry me

effects.log: {npc} laughs. "That is the clever answer," {he} says. "Not the true one." {He} leaves the saddle on the stone. You can feel the bone in your horn agree with {him}, and that is the worst of it.

choices.text: Stand still and let {him} see you are not going to answer

effects.log: {npc} waits until dark. Then {he} gets up and goes, and leaves the saddle, and the two grooms, and says over a shoulder, "When it is ready, it will come."

choices.text: Lower your head and let {him} put a hand on the horn

effects.log: {npc} puts a hand on the bone and closes {his} eyes and smiles like someone who has found a sword in the grass. You pull away. Something in you did not want to. (Bent +1: the horn remembers)

events.text: A season of mending: you set yourself to it as you once set yourself to walking lightly. The farmers whose fields you ran through, the creatures you crushed, the wounds you gave. Some of them are dead of old age. Their children are not.

choices.text: Go to the children, then, and mend for them

effects.log: A barn rebuilt, a well cleared, a lame horse walked every morning until it is not lame. The children never know who. The white in your horn goes dull, and then a little pink. (Bent -4; -10 health)

choices.text: Lie in the cave a whole winter and remember each one by name

effects.log: It is not mending. It is something mending starts from. In the spring you go out and the grass on the meadow stands up after you as it did when you were a foal. (Bent -2)

choices.text: It is done. The horn is what you made it. Walk on

effects.log: You walk on. You cannot unbend grass by looking at it. That is true, and it is also the kind of true thing a horn of bone would say.

events.text: The saddle is still on the Morning-Heaven Stone, mossy now, and the last old groom still sits beside it, and the warlord's war has come over the hills at last. Smoke on the ridge. From the cave mouth you can see {npc}'s banner, and the gap in the enemy line where a horn would go through, and your own horn throbbing white in the dawn.

choices.text: Kick the saddle into the rapids and go up into the mountains for ten years

effects.log: The saddle goes down the rapids with the moss still on it, and the old groom watches it go and then, slowly, laughs. The war is fought without you. When you come back, the white in your horn has dulled.

choices.text: Walk down into the war and stand between the lines with the bone showing

effects.log: Both armies see the horn. Both are sure you have come for them. You stand between them and do not lower it, all day, and by evening they do not know what you are, and that is enough to stop them. (-20 health)

choices.text: Go to the saddle

effects.log: You walk down to the stone and stand still while the old groom, weeping with joy, saddles you. The warlord rides you through the gap in the line with your horn lowered and the bone bare, and the armies follow the horn. It is over in a day. You are a magnificent beast. You are only that, now.

events.text: A bandit chief on the ferry road, {npc}, with a scar through one eyebrow and forty men in the trees. {He} hears you out because a talking beast is new, and then says, "Fine words. My men eat on this road. What do they eat if I sell my horse for a field?"
events.arc: The Bell Voice on the Roads

choices.text: "Barley. I will show you where the soil is good"

mem.note: showed us where the soil was good

effects.log: You walk the hills with {npc} for a week. There is an abandoned valley with good soil and a stream nobody has used since the last war. By spring forty bandits are very bad farmers. By the next spring they are better ones.

choices.text: "Less than now. And they will live to be old"

effects.log: {npc} laughs and does not answer, and the next month the ferry road is quiet. Nobody knows why. Somebody, very far off, has a field.

choices.text: Stand in the road. Let them rob you, if they can find anything

effects.log: They search you, very gingerly. They find dew. {npc} sits on a stone and laughs until {he} cries and lets the next three travellers go for nothing, in a good mood.

events.text: A swordsman on the river road, {npc}, walking very fast, with a blade wrapped in cloth and a name on {his} lips. Twenty years of training for one morning. The man who killed {his} family is at an inn three villages on, and old now, and has grandchildren.
events.arc: The Bell Voice on the Roads

choices.text: "Go and look at the grandchildren first"

mem.note: told me to look at the grandchildren

effects.log: {npc} goes. Looks. Sits in the inn yard all day with the blade across {his} knees and the old man's grandchildren playing round {him}. At dusk {he} goes away without unwrapping it. It is not forgiveness. It is something with room in it.

choices.text: "I cannot stop you. I will be standing in the inn yard"

effects.log: You are. {npc} comes into the yard and sees heaven's beast standing between {him} and the old man's door, and stands there a long time, and then sits down in the dust and cries for the first time in twenty years.

choices.text: Walk beside {him} the three villages and say nothing at all

effects.log: Three villages with a silent beast at your side is a long time to think. By the third, {npc} is walking slower. At the inn {he} asks for a room, and sleeps, and leaves in the morning by the other road.

events.text: The provincial executioner, {npc}, is washing a broad blade in the river at dawn, as {he} has every week for thirty years. {He} sees you on the water and does not stop washing. "I know," {npc} says. "You need not say it. It is my office. Somebody has to."
events.arc: The Bell Voice on the Roads

choices.text: "Does somebody?"

mem.note: asked whether somebody has to

effects.log: {npc} stops washing. "Somebody has, so far," {he} says, slowly. Two years later a black-robed judge in that province ends the cruel questioning in the courts and halves the hangings, and {npc} retires to grow melons, and sends the judge one every summer.

choices.text: Lie down on the bank and keep {him} company while {he} washes

effects.log: You do not say anything. {npc} washes the blade and then sits beside you on the bank, and talks about each one of them, by name, the whole morning. Nobody has ever asked {him} to. You did not either. You just stayed.

choices.text: "It is your office. It is also your hand"

effects.log: {npc} looks at the hand. "Yes," {he} says. "That is why I wash it in the river and not in a bucket." You did not expect to learn something from an executioner. You do.

events.text: A child herding geese on the dyke, {npc}, sees you and does not run, and asks the question every child asks eventually. "Are you real? My grandmother says you only come when everything is good. Nothing is good. So you cannot be real."
events.arc: The Bell Voice on the Roads

choices.text: "I am real. That means something is good. Look round and find it"

mem.note: told me to find what was good

effects.log: {npc} looks round, frowning, very seriously. "The geese," {he} says finally. "The geese are good." You agree that the geese are good. It is the beginning of something.

choices.text: "Your grandmother is right. I came anyway"

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it and decides this is the most interesting thing that has ever happened, and tells everyone, and is not believed, and does not care.

choices.text: Let the child touch your horn and decide

effects.log: A small cold hand on the soft tip of your horn. "Warm," {npc} says, astonished. The geese have wandered off. You help round them up.

events.text: Two sects on a stone bridge over a gorge, one at each end, swords out, a quarrel three generations old about who may cross first. The elder of one side, {npc}, is the one who has to decide whether to start it. You walk out to the middle of the bridge.
events.arc: The Bell Voice on the Roads

choices.text: "Cross together, then"

mem.note: told us to cross together

ok.log: {npc} and the other elder look at each other across the gorge, and then, very stiffly, walk out to meet you in the middle, and cross together, side by side, with you between. Their disciples follow in a state of shock. They settle it in tea.

fail.log: A young hothead on the far side answers you with a thrown knife. You do not answer that. The elders, ashamed, put their swords up anyway, for today. (-10 health)

choices.text: Lie down in the middle of the bridge. Nobody crosses first now

effects.log: Nobody can cross at all. The two sects stand at the two ends for a day, and then a second, and on the third {npc} sends across a message about a ferry. It is the first message in three generations.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the quarrel was about to begin with

effects.log: {npc} opens {his} mouth and shuts it. Nobody on either end of the bridge knows. You let the silence do the rest.

events.text: A magistrate of the county, {npc}, has a reputation for clearing cases fast. You find out how in the courtyard of the yamen at night: the cudgels, the leg-screws, the confessions. {npc} comes out with a lamp to see what the guards are staring at, and sees you standing in the middle of the yard among the instruments.
events.arc: The Bell Voice on the Roads

choices.text: "Every confession in this yard is a lie you paid for"

mem.note: said every confession was paid for

ok.log: {npc} looks at the leg-screws in the lamplight for a long time. In the morning they are burned in the yard. The county's cases go very slowly after that. Fewer of them are wrong.

fail.log: {npc} has the guards drive you out with torches. You go. But the guards were watching, and one of them, years later, will be the one who testifies.

choices.text: Stand there till dawn, so every prisoner brought out sees you

effects.log: Nobody is put to the question in that yard that night, because nobody can do it with heaven's beast watching. It is one night. You know it is only one night. Someone has to start counting.

choices.text: Lie down by the cells and keep the prisoners company

effects.log: All night, at the bars. The prisoners whisper their names to you. You remember every one, and think of the black ribbon of the Judge as if it were already tied.

events.text: A frog on the path in the dark, the colour of the path. Your hoof is already coming down.

choices.text: Stop it in the air

ok.log: Your hoof stops a finger's width above the frog. The frog, unimpressed, hops into the ditch. Centuries of practice for one frog. Worth it.

fail.log: Not fast enough. You stand over the small flat thing in the dark for a long time. (Bent +1)

choices.text: Step onto the air over it, as if it were water

effects.log: You do not need the path. The frog never knows anything passed over it.

events.text: A procession of caterpillars crossing the dyke in single file, nose to tail, a hundred of them, and a farmer behind you on the dyke with a cart who needs to get by.

choices.text: Wait. The farmer can wait too

effects.log: The farmer waits, and swears, and then, because you are so obviously waiting, starts counting caterpillars. It is a hundred and twelve. The farmer tells the village. The village thinks the farmer has been drinking.

choices.text: Lift the farmer's cart over them on your back

effects.log: The farmer rides heaven's beast with a cart of turnips across a line of caterpillars. Nobody in that village is ever believed about anything again.

choices.text: Let the farmer pass; caterpillars are many (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: The cart goes over. Most of them are fine. Not all. You know which. (Bent +1)

events.text: A swallow's nest in the eaves of the temple gate, so low that you would have to duck to pass under it, and the fledglings have just this morning decided to try their wings, which they are bad at. One is on the ground in front of you, flapping.

choices.text: Lie down and wait for the parents

effects.log: The parents come, furious, and herd the fledgling back up by some method you cannot follow. You lie in the gate all morning, and the monks step over you.

choices.text: Lift it back to the nest on the flat of your horn

effects.log: The fledgling sits on your horn tip as if it had always meant to, and steps off into the nest. The temple records it. The swallows come back to that gate every spring for generations.

events.text: The summer rains do not stop. The river comes over the dykes in the night and the whole valley below the ridge is brown water to the eaves. On the roofs, families. On the one hill, a temple full of people with no food. The boats have all gone downstream, empty, without anyone in them.

choices.text: Walk out on the flood, roof to roof, and bring them to the hill

effects.log: All day and all night, a family at a time, walking on the water with them clinging to your back and to your tail and to each other. Nothing under you is crushed. The roofs empty one by one. (-10 health)

choices.text: Carry food from the high villages to the temple on the hill, across the water

effects.log: Sacks of millet, a pot of soy, a basket of dried fish, ferried on your back over the brown water. The temple eats. The monks write it down as a miracle. It was mostly logistics.

events.text: On the third day the water is still rising and the temple hill is getting smaller. The only high ground is the ridge across the valley, and between, a mile of moving water. Two hundred people on the hill. They have seen you walk on it. They are looking at you.

choices.text: Lead them across, all of them, walking on the water behind you

ok.log: They walk on the water behind you, in a column, holding each other's sleeves, and the water holds them as it holds you, as long as they do not look down. Nobody looks down. Two hundred people on the ridge by dusk, and a story that will outlive the dynasty.

fail.log: It holds the first fifty. Then someone looks down. You go back for every one who goes in, and you get them all, but it takes all night and the cold water, and you come out on the ridge at dawn shaking. (-15 health)

choices.text: Carry them across, a few at a time, all night

effects.log: Forty crossings. You stop counting at thirty. By morning the hill is empty and the flood has its top, and you lie on the ridge among two hundred wet people who keep putting blankets on you. (-20 health)

events.text: The flood goes down. Mud to the knee over every field, dead oxen in the ditches, houses leaning. In the mud of the lowest field, by the broken dyke, the farmers find a line of hoofprints that goes out across the water's old surface and stops in the middle of nothing, in the air, where the flood used to be.

choices.text: Help them rebuild the dyke, stone by stone

effects.log: A whole autumn. The dyke is higher than it was and the stones are set so well that the village thinks the mountain god did it. You let them. (-8 health)

choices.text: Go round the valley and lead the drowned animals' young to dry pasture

effects.log: Calves, kids, a foal, a litter of piglets in a trough. You find them all, or nearly all, and bring them up to the ridge, where the farmers stand looking at a beast of heaven herding piglets.

choices.text: Leave them to it. Floods are what rivers do

effects.log: You go back to the cave. The valley rebuilds on its own, slowly, and does it well. You were needed for three days. Not for the rest. That is how it should be.

events.text: A generation later, in the flood valley, there is a custom you did not start: at the summer festival the children walk out along the top of the dyke in a line, holding each other's sleeves, very carefully, not looking down. They do not know why. Their grandparents do.

choices.text: Walk along the dyke with them, at the end of the line

effects.log: The last child in the line feels something take the end of the sleeve, and looks back, and screams, and then laughs, and the whole line looks back, and the grandparents on the bank stand up all together.

choices.text: Watch from the ridge

effects.log: You watch from the ridge. They do not look down. It is enough to know they have a reason not to.

events.text: You walk down a long river for the first time, on it, mile after mile, until you come to a valley between two ridges where the water turns blue-green and very cold, and something under it notices you. The river is not empty. The river belongs to someone, and the someone is old and proud and has a ridge for a back.

choices.text: Stop, step off onto the bank, and bow to the water

effects.log: The water goes still under the rain. Then, very slowly, a ripple runs up the whole length of the river toward you and stops at your hooves, like a nod. The Azure Dragon does not come up. It does not need to.

choices.text: Walk on, lightly. You are crushing nothing; it is anyone's water

effects.log: The rain gets heavier with every step you take, until it is coming down so hard you cannot see the banks. It is not an attack. It is a dragon making a point. You walk out of its valley soaked, and amused, and a little ashamed.

choices.text: Stand on the water and wait to be noticed properly

effects.log: You wait. A day. The river under you is very deep. On the second day a great blue-green eye opens under the surface, right below your hooves, and looks at you, and looks at the grass on the bank, standing straight where you passed, and closes again.

events.text: The valley between the ridges has a drought, though the river is full. The dragon will not give rain this year; the villages have been cutting the ridge's trees and you can see the scars. A rain-rite in the village, drums, a painted dragon of straw carried round the fields, and nothing. The headman sees you on the river and comes down the bank on his knees.

choices.text: Go upriver and ask the dragon for them

effects.log: You stand on its water a whole night. In the morning the rain comes, a little, enough. And on the ridge the woodcutters find that every stump they cut has a green shoot from it, and stop cutting. The dragon was not asking for rites. It was asking for its trees.

choices.text: Tell the headman the truth: the trees

effects.log: The headman goes white, and then goes up the ridge with the whole village and plants saplings for a month. The rain comes in the autumn. You feel the river, under you, approve.

choices.text: It is not your valley. Walk on

effects.log: You walk on. The village and the dragon sort it out between them, after a hard year. Valleys do.

events.text: Thunder on the left ridge, and a voice in it you have heard before, through water. The Azure Dragon is speaking to you directly at last, and it is not polite, but it is not unkind. "A beast that walks on my river and bends nothing," it says. "Come to the council of the Spirits one day, and I will say I saw it."

choices.text: "I will try to be worth saying it about"

effects.log: The thunder rolls once more, which you choose to take as a laugh. On the left ridge, in the morning, there is a stand of pine where no pine was, as if the dragon had wanted to leave a mark.

choices.text: "Say what you saw. No more"

effects.log: "Proud," the thunder says. "Good. A seat is no place for something that is not." The storm goes off east, and you are wet to the ribs, and pleased.

events.text: In the capital the king has a new consort, and the court has gone strange: executions over small things, feasts that go on for days, ministers who disappear. You go to the palace roof at night and look down through the lattice, and the consort, alone in the hall, looks straight up at you, and on the screen behind, the lamp throws a shadow with far too many tails.
events.arc: The Consort With Too Many Shadows

choices.text: Stay on the roof and let the fox know you have seen

effects.log: The consort smiles up at the lattice. It is the smile of the fox who bit your ear when you were young, all grown up. Hello, it mouths. You do not answer. You do not leave either.

choices.text: Come down into the hall

effects.log: You come down through the lattice into the hall, and the consort laughs out loud and sits back on the cushions. "There you are," it says, in a voice you know. "I wondered how long."

events.text: The fox speaks through the consort's mouth, lazily. "I will make you an offer, old friend. Every minister I eat deserves it, and the king will be dead in a year whatever you do. Stay out of my palace and I will give you the next reign: the good prince will be crowned, and you can come to the coronation and be a sign. I do the killing. You stay clean. Everyone wins."
events.arc: The Consort With Too Many Shadows

choices.text: "No"

effects.log: "No," the fox repeats, savouring it. "Still. You are the most tiresome creature I have ever met. Very well. Try and stop me without a horn." It is the only compliment it has ever paid you.

choices.text: "You would not be doing it for me. Do not pretend you would"

effects.log: The consort's smile goes, for a moment, and the fox looks out of it, old and hungry and lonely. "No," it agrees. "But it would be nice if you thought so." Then the smile is back.

choices.text: Stand in the hall all night so that no minister is eaten tonight

effects.log: The fox cannot do it with you watching. It does not like being watched. In the morning it yawns and says it will go somewhere less boring, and does, within the year, and the king lives. Nobody knows why the consort left. (-10 health)

events.text: Years later, on a mountain road, a fox with too many tails sits on a stone and watches you go by, and does not insult you, or bite you, or steal anything. You stop. It says, "I have been thinking about that hall. Whatever you did in it, it was pointless. I would have gone anyway."
events.arc: The Consort With Too Many Shadows

choices.text: "I know"

effects.log: The fox looks at you sideways for a long moment, and then laughs, and goes off down the road, all its tails in the air. You think, not for the first time, that it would be a very good friend if it ever let itself.

choices.text: Lie down on the road beside the stone for a while

effects.log: The fox pretends not to notice. After a while it lies down too. Two old things in the sun on a mountain road, not talking. It is the most peaceful hour either of you has had in a century.
